title: Agent-assisted experimental strategy transfer across quantum processors
authors: Shi-Yao Hou, Zipeng Wu, Chao Zhang, Guanru Feng, Keren Li, Jingen Xiang
abstract: Progress in quantum hardware requires a growing volume of experiments across diverse devices, straining the capacity of human experts. Automation remains challenging because device differences and drift can render workflows developed on one processor unsuitable for another. Here we present an agent-assisted experimental strategy for conducting experiments across three-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance processors. Developed on one processor and applied sequentially to four others, the strategy uses an agent to assess experimental evidence, select subsequent measurements and adapt procedures, with operators providing instrument preparation and physical intervention. Using three-qubit Grover state preparation as a common task, each deployment combined device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization and measurement. The experimental strategy was refined through sequential deployment, and all four processors ultimately produced outputs dominated by their respective marked states. The marked-state populations of the reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranged from \(0.910\) to \(0.959\), with relative deviations below \(3.8\%\) from the ideal value of 0.945. These results demonstrate that an agent-assisted experimental strategy can be reused and refined across processors to realize a common quantum task, providing a basis for scaling experimental practice beyond individual devices.
summary: This paper introduces an agent-assisted methodology to enable the transfer and refinement of quantum experimental protocols across multiple, disparate quantum processors. By using an agent to guide adaptive measurements, the authors successfully executed a three-qubit Grover state preparation task on four different NMR systems. This demonstrates a scalable approach to quantum experimentation that mitigates the challenges posed by device heterogeneity.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is the difficulty of transferring complex quantum experimental workflows between different quantum processors due to inherent device variations and time-dependent drift.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated an agent-assisted strategy that could be reused and refined across multiple distinct quantum processors to execute a common multiqubit task with high fidelity.
method: They employed an agent-assisted framework that separates a transferable experimental strategy from device-specific physical realization, guiding sequential measurements and adaptations.
model_or_system: The experiments were conducted on three-qubit Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) processors, using three inequivalent fluorine nuclei. The task was three-qubit Grover state preparation, requiring local calibration and pulse optimization for each deployment.
key_observables: Marked-state populations of reconstructed dominant eigenstates, Total-Variation (TV) distances from ideal distributions, and reference quality metrics.
important_parameters: The ideal marked-state population for the Grover task was $121/128 \simeq 0.945$. Relative deviations across processors were kept below 3.8%.
main_assumptions: The T2T (Target-to-Task) component of the strategy was not evaluated, and the agent's context isolation required procedural restrictions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the agent coordination, the T2T/T2E framework, and the sequential transfer of the strategy across four processors, showing final marked-state populations and TV distances.
paper_structure: The paper details the development of the agent-assisted strategy, its application to the three-qubit Grover task across multiple processors (Q0 to Q3), and the rigorous diagnostics used to assess performance and repeatability.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, operational framework for scaling quantum experiments beyond single devices by automating the adaptation process, which is crucial for advancing hardware-agnostic quantum algorithms.
